resources.string: These are core Android processes, such as System UI, telephony, your keyboard, Play services and the launcher. Force-stopping one can freeze the UI, break notifications or calls, or require a restart.\n\nOnly continue if you understand the risk and really want to close one of these yourself.

%s manages background apps more aggressively than stock Android. It can silently stop Killora's automation part-way through.

Allowing Killora to ignore battery optimization keeps the automation reliable. If your phone has an Autostart option, enable it for Killora too.

You can change this later in Killora › Settings.

Your apps were already closed the normal way. Deep force stop goes one step further for apps that are still holding something open.

To do that, Killora uses Android's Accessibility Service to open each app's App info screen in Settings and tap the real Force stop button for you.

• It only acts while you are closing apps, and only inside Settings.
• It does not read or collect anything else on your screen.
• Nothing leaves your device.

You can turn it off at any time in Android Settings › Accessibility. On the next screen, find Killora and switch it on.

By default, \"Close selected\" asks Android\'s own ActivityManager API to kill each app\'s background process - no permissions, no Settings screens, the same call on every phone brand. It only affects apps already idling in the background, which is what Android allows any app to do.

Killora opens each app\'s Settings page for you instead of tapping Force stop itself. Tap it yourself, go back, and the next app opens automatically. Nothing is tapped or scrolled on your behalf, and Accessibility is not needed.
